---
title: "Tutorials"
---

The tutorials combine explanation, maintained Python and C++ source code, and
output produced by pySEB during the documentation build.

Follow the numbered learning path below, or jump to the stage that matches
your experience. Within each stage, tutorials appear in a suggested order.
For interactive 3D views, see [Viewing structures](#viewing-structures).

## 1. Start here

**Before starting:** No prior pySEB experience is required. Follow these three
tutorials in order:

| Step | Tutorial | What you will learn |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Introduction to pySEB](introduction.qmd) | Understand scattering, subunits, reference points, structure graphs, parameters, and q |
| 2 | [Your first scattering model](first-model.qmd) | Install pySEB, evaluate a solid sphere, make a plot, and change its radius |
| 3 | [Your first composite model](diblock-copolymer.qmd) | Connect two Gaussian polymers and use the same structure from Python and C++ |

## 2. Build larger structures

**Before starting:** Complete Your first composite model, or be comfortable
adding subunits, linking reference points, and supplying model parameters.

| Tutorial | What you will learn |
| --- | --- |
| [Sphere–polymer micelle](micelle.qmd) | Attach tagged chains to distributed sphere-surface references |
| [Random-walk rod chain](random-walk-rods.qmd) | Link rigid segments, calculate the chain size, and compare with a Gaussian polymer |
| [Reusable nested structures](nested-structures.qmd) | Build reusable graphs and address nested reference paths |
| [Parameter sweeps](parameter-sweeps.qmd) | Reuse one graph with several parameter sets |

## 3. Understand the calculations

**Before starting:** Be comfortable evaluating a composite model and changing
its parameters. Basic familiarity with symbolic algebra is useful for expression
export.

| Tutorial | What you will learn |
| --- | --- |
| [Scattering quantities](scattering-quantities.qmd) | Compare normalized and unnormalized form factors, amplitudes, phase factors, and size measures |
| [Symbolic expressions and export](symbolic-expressions.qmd) | Select a backend, inspect expressions, convert to SymPy, and export Python, LaTeX, and C forms |

## 4. Extend your models

**Before starting:** Be comfortable building composite structures and evaluating
their scattering. The PDB and mixed-model tutorials introduce numerical subunits
alongside analytic models.

| Tutorial | What you will learn |
| --- | --- |
| [Subunits and YAML models](custom-yaml-workflow.qmd) | Understand and explore bundled subunits, then define, validate, and visualize your own |
| [PDB cloud with an attached polymer](pdb-polymer.qmd) | Combine coordinate-based numerical scattering with an analytic subunit |
| [Evaluate mixed models](mixed-model-evaluation.qmd) | Evaluate structures containing numerical, integrated, and analytic subunits with one API |

## 5. Fit experimental data

**Before starting:** Be comfortable building models and exploring parameter
sets. Basic familiarity with least-squares fitting is useful. For the titin
example, first work through PDB cloud with an attached polymer.

| Tutorial | What you will learn |
| --- | --- |
| [Fit real contrast-variation SANS data](fit-real-sans-data.qmd) | Fit a linked sphere-and-shell structure simultaneously to three experimental datasets |
| [Build and fit a polymer corona](fit-f127-corona.qmd) | Connect subunits, view OpenUSD structures, and compare fitted corona models |
| [Fit a linked titin doublet](fit-linked-titin.qmd) | Stress-test analytical domain/linker choices, then compare C-alpha and heavy-atom clouds using real SAXS data |

**Before starting:** Work through Build larger structures, particularly reusable

These are worked applications of the modeling tools, grouped by publication

| Tutorial | What you will learn |
| --- | --- |
| [Figure 10 linear chains](figure10-linear-chains.qmd) | Compare endpoint and distributed-contour links across polymers, rods, loops, and rings |
| [Figure 11 dendrimers](figure11-dendrimers.qmd) | Build branched structures recursively and compare endpoint and contour attachment |

## Viewing structures

The Python tutorials call `pyseb.visualize(world, "structure", parameters)`
after the topology and dimensions are ready, and again for fitted geometries
where useful. Install the optional viewer in the tutorial environment:

```bash
python -m pip install "pyseb[visualization]"
```

Drag to rotate and scroll to zoom. Hover inside the frame and open the
upper-left settings button to change visibility, colors, transparency, and
reference markers. The camera toolbar remains upper-right.
[Viewer settings and realization choices](../visualization.qmd) describes the
optional controls. Polymer shapes and distributed attachment
points show seeded representative realizations, while scattering calculations
average over their ensembles. Numerical clouds use their stored coordinates.
In executable notebook cells, `_ = pyseb.visualize(...)` displays the view
once and suppresses a second display of its returned figure.

## Reference and alternative formats

These extended guides offer broader coverage and a C++ route through the
examples. They are optional references alongside the learning path.

The established modeling task pages present Python and C++ in parallel. Their
Python blocks execute in the documentation environment, while maintained C++
listings are compiled and their output is captured during the build. The
Subunits and YAML Models tutorial runs in Python and includes the equivalent
portable C++ file APIs.

[Symbolic and numerical scattering with Python](pyseb_tutorial.qmd) covers:

- analytic Gaussian-polymer structures;
- symbolic expressions and vector q evaluation;
- finite-sphere Debye clouds;
- callback-defined numerical subunits;
- PDB parsing and atom parameter profiles;
- mixed numerical and analytic structures.

[C++ modelling tutorials](cpp_tutorials.qmd) compile and run seven C++14
programs:

1. a Gaussian diblock copolymer;
2. a sphere–polymer micelle;
3. reusable nested structures;
4. a random-walk chain of thin rods;
5. a parameter sweep written as CSV;
6. a PDB-derived Debye cloud with an attached polymer;
7. structure inspection and hierarchy diagnostics.

The displayed C++ is included directly from the compiled source files. The
terminal output beneath each program is captured from the executable during
the Quarto render.
